summary: A humorous April 1st RFC that proposes adding a Death flag to TCP, using one bit in the header, to make TCP session narratives smooth and attractive. It is a joke and not a real protocol change.

eli5.summary: A joke: a new flag for TCP that acts like the end of a story. It is not real.

questions: what does tcp dth flag do
subtitle: A humorous TCP flag inspired by anime and manga narrative conventions.

tldr.problem: TCP sessions lack a way to signal that termination is likely to occur soon, making it difficult for end users and applications to understand the narrative of the session.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9401 proposes adding a Death (DTH) flag using one bit in the TCP header. The flag signals impending session termination, inspired by the anime and manga convention of setting a 'death flag' on a character who will soon die.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools' RFC treats narrative tropes as a technical protocol problem, using examples from anime, manga, and films to justify a flag that has no functional impact on TCP behavior.

facts.label: Flag position
facts.value: Fourth bit in TCP control bits field

today: RFC 9401 is an Informational RFC published on April 1, 2023. It is a humorous proposal that has not been implemented, as it is not a real protocol enhancement.

sections.title: The Death Flag in TCP
sections.content: RFC 9401 is an April Fools' document that proposes adding a Death (DTH) flag to TCP. The flag uses the fourth bit in the TCP control bits field to indicate likely termination of the TCP session. The flag was inspired by the anime, manga, and light novel convention of a "death flag," a hint that a character will soon die. For example, a character often dies after expressing excessive confidence, revealing their true identity, or sharing a photograph of their future spouse.
sections.eli5: In anime and manga, characters often act in certain ways right before they die, like bragging or revealing secrets. This joke says TCP should have a flag to warn when a connection is about to fail.

sections.title: The DTH Flag Position
sections.content: The DTH flag occupies the fourth bit in the TCP header's control bits field. This bit position was intentionally selected because the number four in Chinese, Sì, sounds similar to Sǐ, which means "die." The flag is informational and does not require acknowledgement. TCP software that does not support the flag can safely ignore it, and receiving the flag does not require action from the recipient.
sections.eli5: The flag goes in the fourth position of the control bits, chosen because "four" sounds like "die" in Chinese. It is just a signal and does not change how TCP works.

sections.title: When to Send the DTH Flag
sections.content: The RFC provides whimsical examples of when to send DTH. A malicious actor should send it when they suddenly repent from a DDoS attack. A mysterious masked character should send it before removing their mask. Applications with resource issues or diminishing performance should send it. Less capable applications and memory-hogging programs should consider the flag when they start producing error messages or heavily consuming resources. The RFC also recommends sending the flag when accessing a "honeypot" or haunted server. Limiting DTH segments to a few per session is recommended to maximize dramatic effect.
sections.eli5: Send the flag when something bad is about to happen: a character is about to be caught, an app is running out of memory, or a connection to a dangerous server.
